questionText: A carpenter saws a log 3 m 60 cm long into pieces of 45 cm each. Every cut takes him 4 minutes, and he rests for 1 minute between one cut and the next. How long does the whole job take, from the start of the first cut to the end of the last cut?
hints: Find the number of pieces first. Then picture the log: how many cuts make that many pieces, and how many rests fall between the cuts?
Change 3 m 60 cm to 360 cm and divide by 45 to find the number of pieces. The number of cuts is one less than the number of pieces.
A similar job: a 2 m pole cut into 50 cm pieces gives 4 pieces. That needs 3 cuts, with 2 rests between them. At 5 minutes a cut and 2 minutes a rest, the time is 3 × 5 + 2 × 2 = 19 minutes.

stepByStep.text: Change the length to centimetres: 3 m 60 cm = 360 cm.
The last piece is simply what remains, so 8 pieces need 7 cuts. Rests come only between cuts, so there are 6 rests.
Add the cutting time and the resting time: the job takes 34 minutes.

misconceptions.A: This counts 8 cuts and 8 rests, one for each piece. Picture the log: after the 7th cut the last two pieces are already apart.
misconceptions.B: The 7 cuts are right, but this adds 7 rests. He rests only between cuts, so count the gaps between 7 cuts.
misconceptions.C: Lovely counting! 8 pieces need 7 cuts, and 7 cuts have 6 rests between them: 28 + 6 = 34 minutes.
misconceptions.D: This uses 8 cuts. Try it with a short stick: cutting it into 2 pieces takes just 1 cut, so the cuts are one fewer than the pieces.

questionText: Riya glues 8 strips of paper end to end to make one long strip. Each strip is 25 cm long, and at every join the two strips overlap by 15 mm. How long is the finished strip?
hints: Two things need care here: the two lengths are in different units, and the number of joins is not the number of strips.
Write 25 cm as 250 mm. Then count the joins when 8 strips are placed in a row.
A similar chain: 5 strips of 20 cm with a 10 mm overlap at each join. There are 4 joins, so the length is 5 × 200 − 4 × 10 = 960 mm, which is 96 cm.

stepByStep.text: Work in millimetres: each strip is 250 mm, so 8 strips laid end to end would be 2000 mm.
8 strips in a row have 7 joins, and each join hides 15 mm.
1895 mm is 189 cm 5 mm, so the finished strip is 189 cm 5 mm long.

misconceptions.A: Well done! 2000 mm less 7 overlaps of 15 mm leaves 1895 mm, which is 189 cm 5 mm.
misconceptions.B: This takes away 8 overlaps. Count the joins in a row of 8 strips: the two end strips each have a free end.
misconceptions.C: Here the 15 mm was taken away as if it were 15 cm. Change both lengths to millimetres before subtracting.
misconceptions.D: This is the length with no overlap at all. Each join hides a little of the paper, so the strip is shorter than this.

questionText: A rectangular garden is 12 m long and 7 m 50 cm wide. Posts are put all the way round its boundary, 1 m 50 cm apart, with a post at every corner. How many posts are needed?
hints: Think of walking once round the whole boundary from one post to the next until you are back at the start.
Find the distance all the way round the garden in centimetres, then see how many gaps of 150 cm fit into it.
A similar garden: a square of side 6 m with posts 2 m apart. The boundary is 24 m, so there are 24 ÷ 2 = 12 gaps and, because the boundary closes up, 12 posts.

stepByStep.text: Change to centimetres: the garden is 1200 cm by 750 cm.
Find the distance all the way round.
Going round a closed boundary, the last gap ends at the first post, so the number of posts equals the number of gaps: 26 posts.

misconceptions.A: This adds the posts on each side: 9 + 6 + 9 + 6. Each corner post stands on two sides, so it has been counted twice.
misconceptions.B: One more than the gaps is right for a straight fence with two ends. Round a closed boundary the last gap comes back to the first post.
misconceptions.C: This uses only one length and one width. The posts go along all four sides of the garden.
misconceptions.D: Exactly! The boundary is 3900 cm, which is 26 gaps of 150 cm, and a closed loop needs one post for each gap: 26.

questionText: An empty drum can hold 100 litres. Every morning Ravi pours 40 litres of water into it, and every night 25 litres leak out. On which morning does the drum become full for the first time?
hints: The water level goes up and then down each day. Ask yourself at which moment of the day the drum holds the most.
Write the level after each morning and after each night for the first two days, and look at how the morning levels grow.
A similar drum: it holds 50 litres, gains 20 litres each morning and loses 10 litres each night. Morning levels are 20, 30, 40, 50, so it is full on the 4th morning, not the 5th.

stepByStep.text: After each full day and night the drum gains 40 − 25 = 15 litres.
The level just after each morning's pouring is 40, then 55, then 70, then 85 litres on the first four mornings.
After the 4th night the drum holds 85 − 25 = 60 litres.
The next morning's 40 litres bring it to 100 litres, so the drum is full on the 5th morning.

misconceptions.A: This divides 100 by the 15 litres gained in a whole day. The drum is fullest in the morning, before the leak, so list the morning levels.
misconceptions.B: Well reasoned! The morning levels are 40, 55, 70, 85 and then 100 litres, so the drum is full on the 5th morning.
misconceptions.C: This is close. List the level after each morning's pouring and see which morning first reaches 100 litres.
misconceptions.D: This divides 100 by 40 and forgets the leak. Each night 25 litres are lost, so the drum fills more slowly.

questionText: A bottle full of juice weighs 1 kg 350 g. When half of the juice has been drunk, the bottle and the remaining juice weigh 800 g. What does the empty bottle weigh?
hints: Compare the two weighings. What exactly was removed between the first and the second?
Write 1 kg 350 g as 1350 g. The drop from 1350 g to 800 g is the weight of half of the juice.
A similar bottle: full it weighs 900 g, and with half the oil used it weighs 600 g. Half the oil is 300 g, all the oil is 600 g, so the bottle is 900 − 600 = 300 g.

stepByStep.text: Write the first weight in grams: 1 kg 350 g = 1350 g.
The weight that went away is half of the juice.
So all of the juice weighs twice as much.
Take the juice away from the full bottle: the empty bottle weighs 250 g.

misconceptions.A: 550 g is what was drunk, which is half of the juice. Double it to get all the juice, then take that from the full weight.
misconceptions.B: Lovely thinking! Half the juice is 550 g, all of it is 1100 g, and 1350 − 1100 leaves 250 g for the bottle.
misconceptions.C: This halves the full weight. Only the juice was halved; the bottle itself stayed the same.
misconceptions.D: This halves the second weight. Find the weight of half the juice first by comparing the two weighings.

questionText: A plane leaves Mumbai when the clocks in Mumbai show 11:40 p.m. It lands in Dubai when the clocks in Dubai show 1:25 a.m. Dubai clocks are always 1 hour 30 minutes behind Mumbai clocks. How long was the flight?
hints: The two times were read on clocks in different cities. Before finding the gap, put both times on the same city's clock.
When Dubai clocks show 1:25 a.m., Mumbai clocks show 1 hour 30 minutes more. Find that Mumbai time first.

A similar trip: a plane leaves town P at 10:00 p.m. by P's clocks and lands in town Q at 11:00 p.m. by Q's clocks, and Q's clocks are 2 hours behind P's. In P's time it lands at 1:00 a.m., so the flight took 3 hours.

stepByStep.text: Change the landing time to Mumbai time: 1:25 a.m. in Dubai is 1 hour 30 minutes later in Mumbai, which is 2:55 a.m.
From 11:40 p.m. to midnight is 20 minutes.
From midnight to 2:55 a.m. is 2 hours 55 minutes.
20 minutes and 2 hours 55 minutes make 3 hours 15 minutes, so the flight took 3 hours 15 minutes.

misconceptions.A: This is the gap between the two clock readings, but they are on different clocks. Change 1:25 a.m. to Mumbai time first.
misconceptions.B: The time difference was taken away here. Dubai clocks are behind, so the same moment has a later time in Mumbai: add it on.
misconceptions.C: Count the gap from 11:40 p.m. to 1:25 a.m. again in two parts, up to midnight and after midnight, then add the 1 hour 30 minutes.
misconceptions.D: Well done! In Mumbai time the plane lands at 2:55 a.m., and 11:40 p.m. to 2:55 a.m. is 3 hours 15 minutes.

questionText: Meena's watch gains 5 minutes in every real hour. She sets it to the right time at 6:00 a.m. Later the same day her watch shows 7:00 p.m. What is the real time then?
hints: The watch gains 5 minutes for each real hour that passes, so think about how far the watch moves during one real hour.
In one real hour the watch moves 65 minutes. Find how many minutes the watch has moved from 6:00 a.m. to 7:00 p.m.
A similar watch gains 10 minutes every real hour and is set right at 8:00 a.m. When it shows 3:00 p.m. it has moved 420 minutes, which is 420 ÷ 70 = 6 real hours, so the real time is 2:00 p.m.

stepByStep.text: From 6:00 a.m. to 7:00 p.m. the watch has moved 13 hours, which is 780 minutes.
In each real hour the watch moves 60 + 5 = 65 minutes.
Find how many real hours have passed.
12 real hours after 6:00 a.m. is 6:00 p.m., so the real time is 6:00 p.m.

misconceptions.A: Excellent! The watch moved 780 minutes at 65 minutes for each real hour, so 12 real hours passed and it is 6:00 p.m.
misconceptions.B: This takes 5 minutes for each of the 13 hours on the watch. The watch gains 5 minutes in each real hour, and fewer than 13 real hours have passed.
misconceptions.C: A fast watch shows a time later than the real time, so the real time must be earlier than 7:00 p.m., not later.
misconceptions.D: The watch gains 5 minutes in every hour, not just once. Work out how many real hours have gone by.

questionText: Buses leave a depot every 25 minutes. The first bus of the day leaves at 6:40 a.m. How many buses leave the depot before 1:00 p.m.?
hints: Find how long it is from the first bus until 1:00 p.m., taking care as the time passes noon. Then think about whether you are counting gaps or buses.
From 6:40 a.m. to 12:40 p.m. is 6 hours, and 20 minutes more reaches 1:00 p.m. Change this time to minutes.
A similar depot: buses every 20 minutes, the first at 9:00 a.m. Before 10:10 a.m. there are 70 minutes, which hold 3 whole gaps, so buses leave at 9:00, 9:20, 9:40 and 10:00: that is 4 buses.

stepByStep.text: From 6:40 a.m. to 1:00 p.m. is 6 hours 20 minutes, which is 380 minutes.
See how many whole gaps of 25 minutes fit.
So the last bus before 1:00 p.m. leaves 375 minutes after the first, at 12:55 p.m.
There are 15 gaps, and the first bus leaves at the start of the first gap, so 15 + 1 = 16 buses leave.

misconceptions.A: 15 is the number of gaps between buses. The bus at 6:40 a.m. leaves before the first gap, so count it as well.
misconceptions.B: The time from 6:40 a.m. to 1:00 p.m. is more than 5 hours 40 minutes. Count on to 12:40 p.m. first, then to 1:00 p.m.
misconceptions.C: Well counted! 380 minutes hold 15 gaps of 25 minutes, and with the first bus at 6:40 a.m. that makes 16 buses.
misconceptions.D: Check the length of time first: 6:40 a.m. to 1:00 p.m. passes noon and is 6 hours 20 minutes. Then remember to count the first bus.

questionText: A model of a tower is made so that 1 cm on the model stands for 6 m of the real tower. The model is 15 cm tall. A second model of the same tower is made so that 1 cm stands for 4 m. How tall is the second model?
hints: Both models show the same real tower. Find the one thing that does not change, and use it as a bridge between the two models.
Use the first model to find the height of the real tower in metres: 15 lots of 6 m.
A similar pair: a model 8 cm tall where 1 cm stands for 5 m shows a 40 m tower. If 1 cm stands for 2 m instead, the model must be 40 ÷ 2 = 20 cm tall, which is taller than before.

stepByStep.text: Find the real height from the first model.
The real tower is 90 m tall, and in the second model each centimetre stands for 4 m.
Find how many centimetres are needed.
22.5 cm is 22 cm 5 mm, so the second model is 22 cm 5 mm tall.

misconceptions.A: Well done! The tower is 90 m tall, and at 4 m to each centimetre the model needs 22.5 cm, which is 22 cm 5 mm.
misconceptions.B: This makes the second model shorter. When each centimetre stands for fewer metres, more centimetres are needed for the same tower.
misconceptions.C: The two scales were subtracted here. Find the real height of the tower first, then share it out 4 m to a centimetre.
misconceptions.D: This multiplies 15 by 4. The 15 cm belongs to the first scale, so use it with 6 m to get the real height first.

questionText: A carpenter has 6 planks, each 2 m long. He needs pieces that are exactly 35 cm long, and each piece must be cut from a single plank. What is the greatest number of pieces he can cut?
hints: Think about one plank on its own before thinking about all six. What happens to the bit left at the end of a plank?
Change 2 m to 200 cm and find how many whole pieces of 35 cm come from one plank, and how much is left over.
A similar job: 4 rods of 100 cm cut into 40 cm pieces. One rod gives 2 pieces with 20 cm left over, so 4 rods give 4 × 2 = 8 pieces, even though 400 ÷ 40 is 10.

stepByStep.text: See how many whole pieces one plank gives.
One plank gives 5 pieces and has 25 cm left over, which is too short for another piece.
Six planks give six times as many, so the greatest number is 30 pieces.

misconceptions.A: This divides all 1200 cm by 35 cm. That would need the short leftover ends of different planks to be joined, which is not allowed.
misconceptions.B: This rounds 1200 ÷ 35 up. A piece cannot be made from part of a length, and the leftover ends cannot be joined.
misconceptions.C: Exactly right! Each plank gives 5 whole pieces with 25 cm to spare, so 6 planks give 30 pieces.
misconceptions.D: This takes 6 pieces from each plank, but 6 × 35 = 210 cm is longer than one plank.

questionText: A sheet of card is 32 cm long and 22 cm wide. Asha cuts small rectangular cards from it, each 80 mm by 50 mm. All the cards are placed the same way round, with their edges along the edges of the sheet. What is the greatest number of cards she can cut?
hints: Whole cards must fit along the length and along the width. Think about rows and columns rather than area, and remember the card can be turned.
Write the card as 8 cm by 5 cm. With the 8 cm side along the 32 cm edge, find how many cards fit along each edge.

A similar sheet: 20 cm by 13 cm, with cards 6 cm by 4 cm. One way gives 3 along and 3 up, which is 9 cards; turned, it gives 5 along and 2 up, which is 10 cards. So the most is 10, although the areas suggest more.

stepByStep.text: The card is 8 cm by 5 cm.
With the 8 cm side along the 32 cm edge: 4 cards fit along the length and 4 rows fit in the 22 cm width, which makes 16 cards.
Turned round, with the 5 cm side along the 32 cm edge: 6 cards fit along the length but only 2 rows fit in the width, which makes 12 cards.
The first way is better, so the greatest number of cards is 16.

misconceptions.A: This divides the areas. After 4 rows a strip 2 cm wide is left along the sheet, and no card fits in it.
misconceptions.B: Well done! Four cards along and four rows up make 16, and turning the card gives only 12.
misconceptions.C: This is the number with the 5 cm side along the long edge. Try the card the other way round too.
misconceptions.D: This adds the 4 along and the 4 up. The cards sit in 4 rows of 4, so multiply.

questionText: 3 mangoes and 2 guavas together weigh 1 kg 150 g. 2 mangoes and 3 guavas together weigh 1 kg 50 g. All the mangoes weigh the same and all the guavas weigh the same. What does one mango weigh?
hints: A mango and a guava do not weigh the same, so sharing equally will not do. Look at what you get by putting the two weighings together, and by comparing them.
Add the two weighings: you then have 5 mangoes and 5 guavas. What do one mango and one guava weigh together?

A similar puzzle: 2 apples and 1 pear weigh 500 g, and 1 apple and 2 pears weigh 400 g. Together that is 3 apples and 3 pears for 900 g, so one of each is 300 g. Swapping a pear for an apple adds 100 g, so an apple is 200 g and a pear is 100 g.

stepByStep.text: In grams the two weighings are 1150 g and 1050 g. Together, 5 mangoes and 5 guavas weigh 2200 g, so one mango and one guava weigh 440 g.
The first weighing has one mango in place of a guava and is 100 g heavier, so a mango weighs 100 g more than a guava.
Two mangoes weigh 440 g and 100 g more.
Halve it: one mango weighs 270 g.

misconceptions.A: This shares 1150 g equally among 5 fruits, but a mango and a guava have different weights. Compare the two weighings instead.
misconceptions.B: This is the weight of one guava. The question asks for the mango, which is the heavier fruit.
misconceptions.C: This is half of what one mango and one guava weigh together. The mango is 100 g heavier than the guava, so it is more than half.
misconceptions.D: Lovely reasoning! A mango and a guava together weigh 440 g and the mango is 100 g heavier, so the mango weighs 270 g.

questionText: A candle 24 cm tall burns down by 3 mm every 5 minutes. It is lit at 10:50 a.m. At what time will the candle be exactly 6 cm tall?
hints: Read carefully what the 6 cm is: the part that has burned, or the part that is still standing?
Find how much of the candle must burn away, and write it in millimetres so that it matches the 3 mm.
A similar candle: 10 cm tall, burning 2 mm every 3 minutes, lit at 11:30 a.m. To be 4 cm tall it must lose 60 mm, which is 30 lots of 2 mm and takes 90 minutes, so the time is 1:00 p.m.

stepByStep.text: Find how much must burn away, in centimetres.
18 cm is 180 mm. Find how many lots of 3 mm that is.
300 minutes is 5 hours, and 5 hours after 10:50 a.m. is 3:50 p.m., so the candle is 6 cm tall at 3:50 p.m.

misconceptions.A: This is the time when 6 cm has burned away. The question wants 6 cm to be left, so find how much has to burn.
misconceptions.B: This is when the whole candle has burned. Stop when 6 cm is still standing.
misconceptions.C: Well done! 18 cm must burn, which takes 300 minutes, and 5 hours after 10:50 a.m. is 3:50 p.m.
misconceptions.D: This counts 180 minutes, one minute for each millimetre. The candle takes 5 minutes for every 3 mm.

questionText: Asha's steps are 60 cm long and her father's steps are 90 cm long. They start with their heels on the same line and walk 36 m in the same straight direction. Counting the starting line, at how many places do their heel marks fall on the same spot?
hints: Asha's heel lands on multiples of one number and her father's on multiples of another. Where can both land?
List Asha's first few marks (60 cm, 120 cm, 180 cm) and her father's (90 cm, 180 cm) to find the first spot they share after the start.
A similar walk: steps of 40 cm and 60 cm over 6 m. The marks meet every 120 cm, at 0, 120, 240, 360, 480 and 600 cm. That is 600 ÷ 120 = 5 gaps, so 6 shared places.

stepByStep.text: Asha's marks are at multiples of 60 cm and her father's at multiples of 90 cm. The first distance in both lists is 180 cm.
So their marks fall together every 180 cm. The walk is 36 m, which is 3600 cm.
Find how many gaps of 180 cm there are.
The shared marks are at the start of the first gap and at the end of every gap, so there are 20 + 1 = 21 places.

misconceptions.A: Well spotted! The marks meet every 180 cm, which gives 20 gaps in 3600 cm and, with the starting line, 21 places.
misconceptions.B: 20 is the number of gaps of 180 cm. The question counts the starting line too, where both heels begin.
misconceptions.C: This divides by 60 + 90. The marks meet where a multiple of 60 is also a multiple of 90, so look for common multiples.
misconceptions.D: This is the number of steps the father takes. Only some of his marks are shared with Asha's.

questionText: Kiran drank half of the juice in a jug and then 150 ml more. Later his sister drank half of what was left and then 100 ml more. Now 200 ml of juice is left in the jug. How much juice was in the jug at the start?
hints: The end is known and the start is not, so begin from the 200 ml and undo each thing that happened, the latest first.
Just before the sister drank her last 100 ml, the jug held 200 + 100 = 300 ml. That 300 ml was half of what she found in the jug.
A similar story: Tara spent half her money and then 20 rupees more, and has 30 rupees left. Before the 20 rupees she had 50 rupees, and that was half, so she began with 100 rupees.

stepByStep.text: Put back the sister's last 100 ml.
That was half of what she found, so double it.
That was half of the juice at the start, so double it: the jug held 1500 ml, which is 1 litre 500 ml.

misconceptions.A: Here the amounts were doubled before the extra millilitres were put back. Undo the latest thing first: the extra amount was drunk after the half.
misconceptions.B: This adds everything that is mentioned and doubles once. Each child drank a half, so there are two doublings, one for each.
misconceptions.C: This doubles 200 ml twice and adds the extras at the end. Put back each extra amount before doubling.
misconceptions.D: Well done! Working backwards gives 300 ml, 600 ml, 750 ml and then 1500 ml, which is 1 litre 500 ml.

questionText: A wall clock takes 6 seconds to strike 4 o'clock, timed from the first strike to the last. The gaps between strikes are always equal. How long does the clock take to strike 10 o'clock?
hints: The timing starts on the first strike and stops on the last. Think about what fills the time in between.
Draw 4 dots in a row for the 4 strikes and count the gaps between them. The 6 seconds are shared among those gaps.
A similar clock takes 8 seconds to strike 3 o'clock. Three strikes have 2 gaps, so a gap is 4 seconds. Striking 6 o'clock has 5 gaps and takes 5 × 4 = 20 seconds.

stepByStep.text: Four strikes have 3 gaps between them.
Find the length of one gap.
Ten strikes have 9 gaps between them.
Nine gaps of 2 seconds: the clock takes 18 seconds.

misconceptions.A: This shares the 6 seconds among 4 strikes. The time passes in the gaps between strikes, and 4 strikes have only 3 gaps.
misconceptions.B: Well done! Each gap is 2 seconds, and 10 strikes have 9 gaps, so it takes 18 seconds.
misconceptions.C: The gap of 2 seconds is right, but 10 strikes have 9 gaps between them, not 10.
misconceptions.D: This doubles the 6 seconds. Find the length of one gap first, then count the gaps for 10 strikes.

questionText: A machine is switched on at 9:40 p.m. on Thursday and runs without stopping for exactly 75 hours. On which day and at what time does it stop?
hints: Break the 75 hours into whole days and some hours left over. Whole days bring you back to the same clock time.
72 hours is exactly 3 days. Find the day and time 3 days after Thursday 9:40 p.m., then see what the remaining hours do.
A similar run: a pump starts at 10:30 p.m. on Monday and runs for 50 hours. 48 hours later it is Wednesday 10:30 p.m., and 2 more hours pass midnight, so it stops on Thursday at half past midnight.

stepByStep.text: Split the 75 hours into whole days and extra hours.
Three days after Thursday 9:40 p.m. is Sunday 9:40 p.m.
Three more hours: 2 hours 20 minutes reach midnight, when Monday begins, and 40 minutes remain.
So the machine stops on Monday at 12:40 a.m.

misconceptions.A: The clock time is right, but the last 3 hours pass midnight. Once midnight has passed, a new day has begun.
misconceptions.B: Well done! Three days bring it to Sunday 9:40 p.m., and 3 more hours pass midnight to Monday, 12:40 a.m.
misconceptions.C: Forty minutes after midnight is in the early morning, so it is a.m., not p.m.
misconceptions.D: This is after 72 hours. The machine runs for 75 hours, so 3 more hours must be added.

questionText: A sports camp runs every day from 25 January 2024 to 5 March 2024, counting both the first day and the last day. For how many days does the camp run?
hints: Count the days month by month, and look closely at the year before deciding how long February is.
In January the camp runs on the 25th, 26th, 27th, 28th, 29th, 30th and 31st. Count them, then think about February 2024.
A similar count: from 20 February 2020 to 3 March 2020, both days included. 2020 is a leap year, so February gives 10 days (20th to 29th) and March gives 3, which is 13 days.

stepByStep.text: January: from the 25th to the 31st, both included, is 7 days.
February: 2024 can be divided exactly by 4, so it is a leap year and February has 29 days.
March: from the 1st to the 5th is 5 days.
Add the three parts: the camp runs for 41 days.

misconceptions.A: Well done! 7 days in January, 29 in February because 2024 is a leap year, and 5 in March make 41 days.
misconceptions.B: This is one day short. Check whether 2024 is a leap year, and make sure 25 January itself has been counted.
misconceptions.C: This is two days short. January gives 7 days when both the 25th and the 31st are counted, and February 2024 has 29 days.
misconceptions.D: This is one day too many. January has 7 camp days, from the 25th to the 31st, and February 2024 has 29.

questionText: A pile of 200 sheets of paper is 1 cm 6 mm thick. A book made of this paper has 350 numbered pages, with one page on each side of every sheet, and two covers that are each 1.5 mm thick. How thick is the book?
hints: Pages and sheets are not the same thing. Decide how many sheets of paper the book really has before working out any thickness.
Each sheet has a page on its front and a page on its back, so halve 350 to find the number of sheets. Then compare that with the pile of 200 sheets.
A similar book: 100 sheets make a pile 9 mm thick. A book of 400 pages has 200 sheets, which are 18 mm thick, and two covers of 1 mm each bring it to 20 mm.

stepByStep.text: Find the number of sheets in the book.
The pile of 200 sheets is 16 mm thick, so 25 sheets are 2 mm thick.
Add the two covers: the book is 17 mm thick.

misconceptions.A: This uses 350 sheets. A sheet has a page on each side, so 350 pages need only half as many sheets.
misconceptions.B: This is the paper alone. The book also has two covers, each 1.5 mm thick.
misconceptions.C: Well done! 175 sheets are 14 mm thick, and the two covers add 3 mm, which makes 17 mm.
misconceptions.D: Only one cover has been added here. A book has a front cover and a back cover.

questionText: Two clocks are set to the right time at 12 noon. One gains 3 minutes every hour and the other loses 2 minutes every hour. What time does the fast clock show when the two clocks are exactly 1 hour apart for the first time?
hints: Think about how quickly the two clocks move apart from each other, then about what the question finally asks you to read.
Each hour one clock goes 3 minutes ahead and the other falls 2 minutes behind, so the gap between them grows by 5 minutes an hour.

A similar pair, set right at 6:00 a.m.: one gains 4 minutes an hour and one loses 1 minute an hour. They are 20 minutes apart after 20 ÷ 5 = 4 hours, at a real time of 10:00 a.m., when the fast clock shows 10:16 a.m.

stepByStep.text: Find how fast the gap between the clocks grows each hour.
Find how many hours it takes for the gap to reach 60 minutes.
12 hours after 12 noon the real time is 12 midnight.
By then the fast clock has gained 36 minutes, so it shows 12:36 a.m.

misconceptions.A: Well done! The gap grows 5 minutes an hour, so it takes 12 hours, and the fast clock is then 36 minutes past midnight: 12:36 a.m.
misconceptions.B: This is the real time when the clocks are an hour apart. The question asks what the fast clock shows, and it is ahead of the real time.
misconceptions.C: This is what the slow clock shows at that moment. The fast clock is ahead of the real time, not behind it.
misconceptions.D: This waits until the fast clock alone is an hour ahead. The other clock is falling behind at the same time, so the gap opens sooner.

questionText: A bottle holds 75 ml of cough syrup. Anu takes 5 ml every morning and 5 ml every night. Her first dose is on Monday night. When does she take the last dose from the bottle?
hints: Count doses rather than days, and notice that the first day is not a full day of medicine.
Find how many 5 ml doses the bottle holds. One of them is used on the first Monday night, and after that she takes two every day.
A similar bottle holds 35 ml and gives 7 doses of 5 ml. If the first dose is on Friday night, the other 6 doses fill Saturday, Sunday and Monday, so the last dose is on Monday night.

stepByStep.text: Find the number of doses in the bottle.
The first dose is on Monday night, which leaves 14 doses.
At 2 doses a day, find how many whole days they last.
Those 7 days are Tuesday to the next Monday, and each ends with a night dose, so the last dose is on the next Monday night.

misconceptions.A: This counts 7 and a half days from Monday morning. The first Monday has only a night dose, so count the doses one by one.
misconceptions.B: After the first night there are 14 doses, which is exactly 7 full days. Count them from Tuesday: the 7th day is Monday.
misconceptions.C: Well done! One dose on the first night and then 14 doses over 7 full days end on the next Monday night.
misconceptions.D: This stops one day early. After the first night there are still 14 doses, which need 7 whole days starting on Tuesday.
